title: The song of Moses and the Lamb (Revelation 15–16)
word: The song of Moses and the Lamb
hookLine: by a sea of glass, they sing: great and marvelous are your works

lines: A SONG ON THE FAR SHORE.
A SEA OF GLASS, MINGLED WITH FIRE.
cards: On the far shore of the Red Sea, the water has just closed. Under it lies the army that chased them; ahead, a desert.

And Moses and the people of Israel sing: "I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." Miriam picks up a tambourine and the women dance.
Now jump to near the end of the Bible. John sees another sea, made of glass and shot through with fire. People stand on it, harps in their hands, through their own long chase.

teach.b: Revelation fifteen calls it "the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb." One song, two names. First, the old song comes back.

Two days ago the beast's crowd borrowed a line from it; here it's sung to God again. Israel sang after coming through the sea out of slavery; these singers sing after the Lamb has brought them through.
John hears the Exodus and the story of Jesus as one song. Second, the words: "Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints."
Not about the singers, or what they survived, or how brave they were.
Third, the song looks outward: "for all nations shall come and worship before thee." They've just escaped, and they're already singing about everybody else coming in. Fourth, what comes next is hard.
In chapter sixteen seven angels pour out bowls, and the plagues sound like Egypt again: sores, water turned to blood, darkness, and unclean spirits like frogs.
Some readers hear the Exodus told once more, on a bigger stage. Twice the text says the people under the plagues still would not repent. So the song isn't sung because life is easy.
In Acts, Paul and Silas sing praises in a prison at midnight. Praise here isn't a reward for things going well.

teach.h: SUNG BETWEEN THE CHASE AND THE DESERT.
teach.b: It's what the rescued do on the shore, between the chase and the desert.

how: Christians sing praise in worship, and some churches sing the words of Revelation 15:3–4 as a canticle; the song at the sea from Exodus 15 also has a place in Jewish morning prayers.

games.q: what does “the song of moses and the lamb” mean?
o: a psalm of Moses mourning Israel's years in the desert
the praise sung beside a sea of glass in Revelation 15
a hymn Jesus sang with his disciples at the Last Supper

games.q: the song of Moses and the Lamb — tap the pairs.

s: the song in Revelation 15 is all about how brave the singers were
every line is about God: his works, his ways, his name.
the song says all nations shall come and worship
they've just escaped, and they sing about everyone else coming in.
the plagues of the bowls have nothing to do with Exodus
sores, water turned to blood, darkness, even spirits like frogs: they echo the plagues of Egypt.

games.q: you've just come through a long chase and you're standing on a sea of glass, harp in hand. bowls of plagues are about to be poured out. what do you do?
o: sing about God's works and ways.
tell the story of what you survived.
stay silent until it's all over.
games.why: they sing the song of Moses and the Lamb, and every line is about God, ending with all nations coming to worship.

practice: Sing a hymn you know, a psalm you've heard sung, or any song that says thank you for the world: out loud if you can, humming or inside you if not.
Don't worry about your voice; let the song be about what's great and good, not about you. If you pray, let it be your prayer; if not, let it simply be a song.

wordCard.voice: The song of Moses and the Lamb. In Revelation fifteen, the song sung beside a sea of glass, echoing Israel's song at the Red Sea: great and marvelous are your works.

orig.note: Greek: a song, an ode. the word for the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb in Revelation 15:3.

carryVoice: Your line: great and marvelous. Every line of the song is about God, not the singers. See you tomorrow.
